title: Private Marks: Smoothing, Lag and What the Volatility Number Hides
summary: A quarterly estimate that moves a third of the way toward reality reports a third of the volatility — and the risk that disappears from the statistics does not disappear from the portfolio.

lesson.body:
A listed share has a price every second, set by people transacting. A private company has a **[[fair-value|fair value]] estimate**, produced quarterly, by the manager who owns it.

Both are called valuations and they are different objects:

**A market price** is what someone actually paid. It incorporates every participant's view and it moves whether anyone likes it or not.

**An estimate** is a considered judgement using comparables, transactions and a discounted cash flow, reviewed by an auditor and sometimes by a third-party valuation firm. It moves when the estimator decides it should.

Neither is inherently better, and they have different failure modes. Market prices overshoot in both directions; estimates lag and smooth. **The problem is not that estimates are wrong — it is that they are then used in statistics that assume they are prices.**

Every [[volatility]] figure, correlation and Sharpe ratio computed on a private portfolio inherits the properties of the estimation process rather than of the assets. That is the subject of this topic, and it is the most consequential measurement issue in alternatives.

**Marks move partway toward reality each quarter, and that partial adjustment is what produces the famously low volatility of private assets.**

The mechanism is ordinary rather than sinister. A valuer looking at a portfolio company in a falling market has genuine reasons for caution: the comparables may recover, the business has not changed, the exit is years away, and a mark that whipsaws serves nobody. So the estimate moves *some* of the way.

Repeat that quarterly and the reported series is a moving average of the true series. Moving averages have two properties that matter enormously here:

**Lower variance.** In the worked example below, marks adjusting a third of the way each quarter reported **34% of the true volatility.**

**Lower measured correlation with anything.** A smoothed series correlates poorly with an unsmoothed one, even when the underlying exposures are identical.

**So a private portfolio's diversification statistics are substantially an artefact of the reporting frequency and the estimation process.** The exposure did not fall. The measurement did.

The honest position is that some of the difference is real — private assets genuinely do not suffer the sentiment swings of daily markets, and long holding periods genuinely reduce the relevance of interim prices. **The dishonest position is putting a smoothed volatility figure into a portfolio optimiser next to a market-priced one.** That is a comparison the arithmetic cannot support, and it systematically recommends more private assets.

**Every risk-adjusted measure has volatility in the denominator, so understating volatility overstates the measure — and the effect is mechanical.**

A strategy returning 12% with 6% reported volatility against a 4% [[risk-free-rate|risk-free rate]] shows a Sharpe ratio of 1.33. If the true volatility is 15%, the honest Sharpe ratio is 0.53. **Same returns, and the apparent quality of the strategy falls by 60% on a measurement correction.**

The same applies everywhere the number is used:

**Portfolio optimisation** allocates more to assets with lower measured volatility, so smoothing produces an allocation recommendation. This is not a subtle bias; it is the dominant one in most institutional models.

**Risk budgets** understate the capital genuinely at risk.

**Beta and correlation** look low, which supports a diversification claim that has not been tested.

**Drawdown statistics** understate what the portfolio would have realised if sold.

There are corrections available — unsmoothing techniques that back out the autocorrelation, or using lagged public proxies — and they consistently produce higher volatility and higher correlation. **A manager who has run them and shows the results is doing something unusual and worth noticing.**

A public market falls and recovers over five quarters: cumulative returns of 0%, −8%, −18%, −10%, +2%. A private portfolio with identical underlying exposure marks a third of the way toward the true value each quarter.
walkthrough: The smoothed series never shows the −18% trough. Its worst point is **−8.6%**, less than half the true drawdown, and it arrives a quarter later.
**Quarterly volatility: 9.63% for the public series against 3.23% for the marks — a ratio of 0.34.**
**Read that carefully: identical underlying exposure, and one reports a third of the risk of the other.** Nothing was misstated. Each individual mark was defensible.

Note the lag as well as the damping. The smoothed series is still falling in the quarter when the public market has already begun to recover — which is why private portfolios report their worst quarters after public markets have turned.

Sanity check worth reusing: **compute the autocorrelation of a private return series.** Genuine market returns are close to zero; a strongly positive figure is the signature of smoothing, and its size indicates how much.

lesson.caption: Which reported statistics smoothing distorts
rows: Understated, often by half or more
Unsmooth the series, or use a lagged public proxy.
Overstated, because volatility is the denominator
Compare against lagged public returns, not contemporaneous ones.
Ask what a forced sale would have realised at the trough.
Sum the betas against several lags of the public series.

lesson.body:
**Optimisers fed smoothed inputs.** Mean-variance optimisation allocates on volatility and correlation, both understated. The output is a recommendation to hold more private assets, generated by the measurement rather than by the economics.

**Comparing a private Sharpe ratio with a public one.** The two denominators were produced by different processes. It is not a like-for-like comparison and it is made constantly.

**Denominator staleness in a fall.** When public markets fall and private marks do not, the private allocation rises as a share of the portfolio without anyone buying anything. This is a genuine operational problem for investors with allocation limits.

**Reading stable marks as low risk.** Stability of the estimate is not stability of the value. The test is what the assets would fetch, and that is only observable on a sale.

**Assuming the lag is symmetric.** Marks tend to fall more slowly than they rise. Whether that is prudence or reluctance is not determinable from outside, and the asymmetry is measurable.

**There is a real argument on the other side, and taking it seriously makes the critique sharper rather than weaker.**

The argument: for an investor who genuinely holds to maturity, interim volatility is noise. A daily price series measures the market's changing sentiment, not the asset's value. If you will not sell, the path is irrelevant and only the terminal value matters. On this view, smoothed marks are closer to economic reality than a public price is, and private assets' apparent stability reflects a genuine absence of forced repricing.

That argument is substantially right, and it has two specific limits.

**You might have to sell.** Capital calls, rebalancing, a change of strategy, a secondary sale for liquidity. The moment a sale is possible, the realisable price matters and the mark does not.

**Even if you never sell, the statistics are still being used.** A Sharpe ratio computed on smoothed marks and compared with a public one produces a wrong conclusion regardless of your holding intention.

**So the defensible position is narrow and worth stating precisely: smoothed marks may be a reasonable estimate of value, and they are not a measure of risk.** Use them for reporting and never as an input to a risk model that also contains market-priced assets.

**Compute the autocorrelation of any private return series.** Near zero is a market-like series; strongly positive is smoothing, and the magnitude tells you how much.

**Ask for volatility computed on unsmoothed returns, or against lagged public proxies.** A manager who has done this and shows it is unusual.

**Never put smoothed and market-priced volatilities into the same optimiser.** The allocation it produces is a function of the measurement difference.

**Ask what realisations achieved against their final marks.** The only external test, and it is a matter of record.

**Ask what the portfolio would have fetched at the worst point of the last drawdown.** Managers rarely have a precise answer, and the quality of the reasoning is itself informative.

items: A private mark is a quarterly estimate produced by the owner, not a price. Both are valid objects with different failure modes: prices overshoot, estimates smooth and lag.
In the worked example, marks adjusting a third of the way each quarter reported 34% of the true volatility and less than half the drawdown, arriving a quarter late.
Understated volatility overstates every risk-adjusted measure: a 1.33 Sharpe on 6% reported volatility becomes 0.53 at a true 15%.
The defensible position is narrow — smoothed marks may be a reasonable estimate of value and are not a measure of risk, so they must never share an optimiser with market-priced assets.

questions.stem: Why do private asset return series show low volatility?
choices: Private companies genuinely have more stable values than listed ones
Marks are estimates that move partway toward true value each quarter, and a moving average has lower variance than the series it averages
Private assets are valued at cost until sale
rationales: Some of this is real — long holding periods and no forced repricing — and it does not account for the size of the difference.
Correct. Partial adjustment each period produces a moving average of the true series, and moving averages have systematically lower variance.
Fair value estimation is the standard, not cost. Cost accounting would produce even less movement and is not what happens.
Auditors review the process; the smoothing arises from the estimation itself.
questions.explanation: The mechanism matters because it tells you the fix: unsmoothing techniques recover the underlying series from the autocorrelation. The volatility is not missing, it has been averaged, and averaging is reversible.

questions.stem: A strategy returns 12% with a 4% risk-free rate. Reported volatility is 6%. What is the reported Sharpe ratio? Two decimal places.
questions.explanation: At a true volatility of 15% the same returns give 0.53 — a 60% reduction from correcting one input. It is the clearest illustration of why the denominator deserves as much scrutiny as the return, and it usually gets none.

questions.stem: Same 12% return and 4% risk-free rate, but the unsmoothed volatility is 15%. What is the corrected Sharpe ratio? Two decimal places.
questions.explanation: 0.53 is a perfectly respectable figure and it supports a completely different allocation decision from 1.33. Nothing about the strategy changed — only the honesty of one input.

questions.stem: What happens when smoothed private volatilities are used in a mean-variance optimiser alongside market-priced assets?
choices: The optimiser corrects for the difference automatically
It systematically over-allocates to private assets, because they appear to offer similar returns with less risk and lower correlation
The results are unaffected as long as returns are accurate
rationales: An optimiser takes its inputs literally. It has no way to know one series was estimated and another was traded.
Correct. Lower measured volatility and lower measured correlation are exactly the two properties an optimiser rewards, so the allocation is generated by the measurement process.
Returns are only half the input. The covariance matrix drives the allocation and it is the distorted half.
The bias runs the other way, and strongly.
questions.explanation: This is the most consequential practical effect of smoothing, and the fix is not complicated: unsmooth the private series, or apply a volatility haircut consistent with observed autocorrelation, before optimising. Both are standard techniques and neither is standard practice.

questions.stem: "We hold to maturity, so interim volatility is irrelevant to us." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — the argument is largely sound for the holding decision, but liquidity needs can force a sale, and the smoothed statistics are still being compared with market-priced ones
False — interim volatility always matters equally to all investors
True — for a genuine long-term holder the path is irrelevant
False — because private assets are more volatile than public ones
rationales: Correct. The holding-period argument has real force and two specific limits: you may have to sell, and the statistics get used in comparisons regardless of your intentions.
Over-correction. An investor with no liquidity needs genuinely is less exposed to path risk.
The strongest version of the defence, and it ignores forced sales and the misuse of the resulting statistics.
Their true volatility is comparable to public equity of similar leverage, not obviously higher — the issue is measurement rather than magnitude.
questions.explanation: The precise position is worth being able to state: smoothed marks may be a reasonable estimate of value and are not a measure of risk. That distinction permits their use in reporting and forbids their use in a risk model alongside traded assets.

questions.stem: Which single diagnostic best detects smoothing in a return series?
choices: Autocorrelation of the returns — near zero for market-like series, strongly positive when marks adjust partially
rationales: The Sharpe ratio is a consequence of smoothing rather than a detector of it.
Correct. Partial adjustment makes each period's return partly a repeat of the last, which is exactly what autocorrelation measures. The magnitude also indicates the degree of smoothing.
Drawdown is understated by smoothing and does not identify it without a comparison.
A high win rate is suggestive and easily produced by other means.
questions.explanation: It is a single calculation on a return series you already have, and it turns a suspicion into a measurement. A first-order autocorrelation above about 0.3 in a quarterly private series is strong evidence, and it is also the input to the standard unsmoothing correction.
